passages.label: A
passages.text: Apollo 13 launched on 11 April 1970 with James Lovell, Fred Haise and Jack Swigert. It was meant to be the third mission to land astronauts on the Moon, at Fra Mauro. Two days later, an oxygen tank exploded about 200,000 miles from Earth. The command module Odyssey began losing oxygen, electricity and water. The lunar landing was abandoned. NASA later described the mission as a successful failure because the landing did not happen. But the crew returned safely. That outcome did not stem from one dramatic idea. It required many people to redefine the objective and work within rapidly changing limits.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Mission Control first had to protect the crew's remaining resources. The lunar module Aquarius became a lifeboat, although it had been made for two people for about 45 hours rather than three people for roughly 90. Ground controllers helped reduce electrical use to one fifth of its normal level and planned how lunar-module power could recharge command-module batteries. Water was more worrying than oxygen. So the crew cut consumption sharply. Controllers also calculated engine burns that would put the spacecraft back on a free-return route. These linked decisions show that teams typically solve emergencies by managing a number of constraints together rather than treating each problem in isolation.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The ground organisation depended on clearly separated responsibilities. Flight directors led shifts and made final operational decisions. Specialists watched individual spacecraft systems, while the capsule communicator, or Capcom, spoke directly with the crew. This structure helped Mission Control coordinate technical knowledge without sending conflicting instructions. Each specialist had to maintain attention to one system and still understand how a proposed action might affect the whole spacecraft. Simulators allowed new procedures to be checked before transmission. The arrangement did not remove disagreement. However, it made it possible to differentiate an urgent warning from a weak possibility and to combine expert judgements into one plan. A different flight director led each shift. When the next shift began, its leader needed to know what the people on the earlier one had found out.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The crew needed to counteract carbon dioxide. They had a square container and a round opening. The two did not fit. The crew’s safety was at stake, and a constructive exchange helped people resolve the problem with things they already had. These dynamics involved sharing information and taking ownership of tasks. Ground staff reached consensus and checked their reservations before the crew tried the plan. The outcome shaped people’s perception of how far a team could work apart. It left a legacy for people who trained afterwards. They could learn how two groups shared one job.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Before re-entry, flight controllers prepared instructions to power up the command module in a relatively short time. They concentrated primarily on equipment fundamental to landing. So the crew could differentiate essential actions from those that could wait. When several demands peak at once, a crew member must be able to voice a concern while a controller checks the available data. Keeping the service module until close to re-entry protected the heat shield. Individual skill helped people accomplish these tasks, and communication practices underlie their ability to coordinate and acknowledge information from others. The crew did not have to rely exclusively on their own tests. Checks on Earth could enhance the instructions.

passages.label: A
passages.text: A patient moves from one hospital team to another, and the receiving worker hears an instruction but is interrupted by a distraction. A nod or gesture may acknowledge that something was said without showing which detail was understood. TeamSTEPPS helps teams coordinate at moments like this, and the United States Department of Defense and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality developed the programme, which uses shared communication tools to make it easier for staff to voice a concern.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Complex care may involve a multi-team system, and a core team works most directly with the patient, while coordinating teams, support services, administrators and temporary response teams contribute different resources. Some groups may work across organisations or meet virtually. Clear structure is fundamental because members need to know who is responsible for each task and how information moves between groups. Problems can stem from an undefined role even when every individual is highly trained. Team leaders organise members, state goals, assign responsibilities, allocate resources and revise the plan as things change.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The training links communication, leadership, situation monitoring and mutual support, and a team can reach consensus about a plan while giving people a way to voice reservations. A constructive check can defuse tension and counteract a mistaken perception about what was said, and the dynamics change when staff agree who has ownership of a task, who can resolve a question and what outcome is at stake. A brief restatement helps people confirm a request without waiting for a disagreement to grow. If the patient needs extra help when moving, for example, the receiving worker can repeat the request so the first worker can confirm it. When circumstances change, a short meeting can let staff revise their shared plan, and a person taking over a task then needs to confirm what has changed and who will check the result before work continues.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Three short meeting tools keep a plan current, and a brief occurs before work begins so members can share the plan, assign roles and anticipate problems. A huddle is called when conditions change and the team has to restore awareness or adjust its approach. A debrief follows activity and examines what went well, what failed and what should change next time. These meetings are typically concise and purposeful. A debrief is not a ceremonial gesture or a long report. Used well, the three tools help teams maintain a shared mental model and prevent an avoidable distraction from becoming a safety threat.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Teams that maintain a shared picture of what is happening can differentiate a confirmed fact from an assumption. Sensitivity to time pressure helps explain why information is sometimes lost at a change of shift. Staff can suggest a check and listen to the answer, rather than assume that a colleague who is typically reliable has heard every word. These habits enhance teamwork because workers tend to act on what they believe they heard. The ability to correct a misunderstanding is fundamental to the conditions that underlie safe care.

R_H3.passageTitle: What Google Learned About Effective Teams

passages.label: A
passages.text: Google's People Analytics researchers launched Project Aristotle to investigate team effectiveness at Google, and the name referred to the idea that a whole can be greater than the sum of its parts. Researchers gathered information about teams and considered many possible explanations, and they expected that a particular mixture of people might explain success. Yet the evidence did not produce a simple membership formula. Variables such as similar personalities or backgrounds did not apparently distinguish the strongest teams in Google's analysis, and the important patterns were found in how members worked together. The project therefore shifted attention from selecting ideal individuals to creating conditions in which ordinary interaction could support demanding work.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The researchers identified five dynamics. Psychological safety meant that members felt safe taking interpersonal risks. Dependability meant completing high-quality work on time. Structure and clarity covered understandable roles, goals and plans. Meaning described personal importance, while impact described the belief that the work mattered and contributed to wider goals, and these dynamics were not more or less interchangeable labels. Each drew attention to a different condition. Psychological safety came first because fear can detract from the exchange of ideas even when a team has excellent technical knowledge.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Psychological safety does not mean that every suggestion is accepted, and it means members can ask a basic question, admit a mistake or voice a difficult concern without expecting humiliation. Google presents statements that help teams discuss this climate, including whether mistakes are held against people and whether it is safe to ask for help. Members of safer teams tend to expose uncertainty earlier, giving the group time to respond, whereas a manager who attacks an idea may obtain silence rather than agreement. In one Google scenario, ideas dried up after a manager publicly rejected a colleague's proposal. At first glance two fairly successful teams can seem more or less alike, even though they operate under somewhat different conditions.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Team dynamics may help explain the outcome even when individuals work in different places. A measure of consensus can miss whether people are able to express reservations. A constructive response can defuse tension and counteract a mistaken perception of a colleague’s role. That can help clarify ownership and resolve a difficult question about what is at stake. A company’s legacy can influence which teamwork habits it recognises. Evidence from one organisation gives a reason to examine those habits in another place, where users and working conditions may differ. The meanings attached to teamwork may also vary.

passages.label: E
passages.text: The results suggest that a basic willingness to voice concerns can enhance how a group uses its knowledge, but the evidence was collected primarily inside one company. Google acknowledges that what appeared fundamental there might carry different weight in another organisation. For the most part, the findings help readers differentiate team habits from assumptions based exclusively on who belongs to the team. An apparently attractive measure, such as a higher revenue figure, can detract from closer analysis if used as the only proof that a particular habit caused the result.

The best teams included identical people in exactly the same roles.
The membership pattern explained every difference without looking at behaviour.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How does the passage distinguish meaning from impact?
options: Meaning measures punctuality, and impact measures exactly the same thing.
Meaning refers to team members' preferred work times, and impact refers to whether people meet those times.
A wider goal matters only when no team member can see a personal reason for the work.
Meaning concerns personal importance, while impact concerns how work contributes beyond the individual.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What alternative explanation should a manager consider if new ideas disappear after public criticism?
options: People may still have concerns or ideas but feel less able to express them.
Everyone who says nothing must have agreed with the rejection.
Ideas disappear only when the team actually has nothing else to discuss.
A decline in ideas proves that each person's technical knowledge declined at the same time.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which situation would count as psychological safety even if a proposed idea was rejected?
options: Managers avoid hearing any new suggestions because agreement is preferable.
An idea must receive approval before the person can ask for feedback.
A member can raise a concern and discuss why a proposal will not be adopted without being humiliated.
A team accepts every suggestion even when its members think it will not work.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why can a constructive discussion matter when people disagree about who should deal with a problem?
options: It allows one person to keep all their assumptions about other people's roles.

It makes every team member automatically agree about every outcome.
A longer conversation eliminates the need to state what is at stake.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What would justify checking the study's ideas in another organisation?
options: The findings came largely from one company, and other work settings may make the conditions matter in different ways.

Working in another place would eliminate the need to ask about local habits.
The largest companies always produce the same kind of evidence about interaction.

questions.prompt: What would be missing if a study used higher revenue as its sole proof that a team habit worked?

A way of showing the number under more headings without collecting new evidence
Evidence that the practice actually helped bring about the result

questions.prompt: A team delivers dependable work but rarely admits mistakes. Which reading fits the different measures in the article?
options: Meeting deadlines proves members can always raise uncertainty.

Completing work reliably can coexist with an atmosphere in which people hesitate to raise problems.
The two observations measure exactly the same feature under different names.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which change would help determine whether team members can raise concerns without assuming that more agreement is always better?
options: Ask how people respond when a concern or mistake is raised and distinguish that from how often the team agrees.
Count silent members as agreeing with every decision and treat the tally as the only result.
Ask each person to repeat the leader's decision and assume speaking has become safer.
Measure only how often work is completed on time.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion best fits both what the researchers found and the limit of the evidence?

A higher financial result establishes the same cause in every team.
Once teams have technical knowledge, the conditions for speaking about concerns are irrelevant.
